words.definition: Grown used to a new climate, place, or situation.
The highest point of something; the peak.
Happening by chance; not essential or built in.
Divinely fragrant or delicious. From ambrosia, the food of the Greek gods, which gave them immortality.
Without a clear shape or form.
A round or oval open-air arena with rising tiers of seats around a central space, used in ancient Rome for gladiator contests and public spectacles.
The heavy iron block on which a blacksmith hammers hot metal into shape.
A ghost, or a ghostlike image of a person.
A mysterious or specialized knowledge, language, or information accessible or possessed only by the initiate. From the Latin arcanus, hidden or closed. Plural: arcana.
A maker or repairer of armor and weapons.
Having to do with the stars.
A diving seabird of northern seas. The great auk, a large flightless species, became extinct in 1844. More in the Chapter 43 Resources.
A pufferfish, which swallows water to swell its body into a spiny ball when threatened.
Crusted with barnacles, small shelled sea creatures that cling to rocks, pilings, and the hulls of ships.
A fashionable four-wheeled carriage with a folding half-hood and two seats facing each other. More in the Chapter 43 Resources.
An old term for a Black African or any dark-skinned person, common in European art and in decorative figures of Black servants. It is now considered offensive.
A piece of armor covering the chest.
The title of the chief Muslim ruler, understood as a successor to the Prophet Muhammad.
Also caulker. A worker who seals the seams of a wooden ship to make it watertight. More in the Chapter 43 Resources.
A merry-go-round. Earlier, a tournament in which horsemen performed exercises and displays.
A small, often ornate box for jewels or valuables. In American usage, also a coffin, so Young’s “casket containing no jewel” carries both meanings.
In Greek mythology, a creature with the head and upper body of a man and the body and legs of a horse.
An officer in the Roman army who commanded about a hundred soldiers.
Imaginary, fanciful, or wildly unrealistic. From the Chimera, the fire-breathing monster of Greek myth made of a lion, a goat, and a serpent.
A fortress, usually on high ground, that protects a city.
The hanging metal tongue inside a bell that strikes it to make it ring.
A small saltwater clam with a ribbed, heart-shaped shell. A cockleshell boat is a small, flimsy one.
A row of columns, usually holding up a roof.
A nautical term for long, curling waves that roll in and break on a beach or reef.
A large sea snail with a spiraled shell that can be blown like a horn. Held to the ear, it seems to hold the sound of the sea.
The completion or fulfillment of something.
A description or map of the whole universe, both heavens and earth.
A lookout platform high on a ship’s mast.
A heat-resistant pot for melting metals. Figuratively, a severe test that changes a person.
A soldier in the Crusades, the Christian military campaigns to take the Holy Land, fought between 1096 and 1291.
A fortune-teller who looks into a crystal ball to see the future.
A prospector in the Alps who climbs into rock clefts to find quartz crystals.
A servant who poured and served wine to a king, a position of great trust. Nehemiah was cup-bearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes, and in Greek myth the youth Ganymede was cup-bearer to Zeus.
Also danse macabre. A medieval image of Death leading people of every rank, from pope and king to child and beggar, in a dance to the grave. See On the danse macabre (Ch 43).
Polite respect, or yielding to someone else’s wishes or judgment.
Separation from the body; existing as a spirit without a body.
A person who predicts the outcome of horse races, elections, or other contests from inside information, or “dope.”
A commander or prince in the Islamic world. More in the Chapter 43 Resources.
Adorned with pearls, or having a pearly sheen.
A mystery or puzzle; a person or thing that is hard to understand.
A man who has been castrated. Eunuchs were employed for centuries to guard harems and to serve as officials in royal courts in the Middle East, China, and Byzantium. See The eunuch (Ch 35).
A mistaken belief, or a flaw in reasoning that makes an argument unsound.
A carved figure, often a woman, mounted on the bow of a sailing ship. See On the figurehead and intuition (Ch 40).
The sky or the heavens, imagined as a solid dome overhead, as in Genesis 1.
Trimmed with flounces, wide strips of gathered or pleated fabric sewn to a skirt or dress.
Feelings that something bad is about to happen.
The forward part of a ship below the deck, where the crew lived. Pronounced “FOHK-sul.”
Silly, trivial, or lighthearted things.
The boatman who rows a Venetian gondola, standing at the stern with a single oar.
Calm and peaceful. From the halcyon, a mythical bird said to calm the sea while it nested on the waves in winter.
A ring of light around the sun or moon, caused by ice crystals high in thin clouds.
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: terraced gardens said to have been built by King Nebuchadnezzar II. No trace of them has ever been found.
The wheel or tiller that steers a ship.
A long-legged wading bird with a downward-curved bill, sacred in ancient Egypt to Thoth, god of writing and wisdom.
Shut in or imprisoned, as if walled up.
Something that cannot be measured, weighed, or judged.
Impossible to understand or interpret.
Long settled in a habit and unlikely to change, as in “inveterate gambler.”
To keel over is to capsize, with the keel, the ship’s backbone along the bottom, turning upward. To list is to lean to one side, usually from water taken on.
words.note: “listing” elsewhere in the novel means making a list; Chapter 43 is added by hand.

words.definition: A stretch of shallow water separated from the sea by a reef or sandbar.
A diseased beggar, especially one with leprosy. More in the Chapter 43 Resources.
Sluggishness, drowsiness, a lack of energy.
Bluish-gray, the color of a bruise. Also furiously angry.
The time from one new moon to the next, about 29.5 days.
A plucked string instrument with a rounded back shaped like half a pear, popular in Europe from the Middle Ages through the 1700s.
A great king or prince in India. From the Sanskrit for “great king.”
A high-ranking official of imperial China.
A jellyfish in its free-swimming, bell-shaped stage, named for the Gorgon of Greek myth whose hair was snakes.
Quick and changeable in mood. From the swift Roman messenger god Mercury and the liquid metal named for him.
Having to do with a change of form. In geology, rock that heat and pressure have changed.
A mineral that splits into thin, shiny, nearly transparent sheets and makes rock glitter.
A tall, slender tower of a mosque, from which the call to prayer is given.
An optical illusion, common in deserts, in which hot air bends light so that distant water or cities seem to appear.
A seasonal wind in South Asia that brings months of heavy rain.
A picture or pattern made by setting small pieces of colored stone, glass, or tile together.
An old or worn-out horse.
The tide with the smallest difference between high and low water, twice a month at the quarter moons. More in the Chapter 43 Resources.
A woman’s light, flowing dressing gown.
In Homer’s Odyssey, a drug from Egypt that Helen puts in the wine to banish grief and sorrow. Anything that brings forgetfulness of pain. See On Nepenthe (Ch 82).
A servant woman or concubine in a Turkish harem. More in the Chapter 43 Resources.
An Asian tiered tower with multiple eaves, usually a Buddhist temple or shrine.
A medieval pilgrim who brought back a palm frond from the Holy Land. More in the Chapter 43 Resources.
A statement or situation that seems to contradict itself and yet may be true.
A light umbrella carried for shade from the sun.
An ornamental garden of flower beds laid out in a pattern. A parterred floor is inlaid in patterned sections.
Walks or strolls, especially leisurely ones.
A journey, especially a long or meandering one.
Ghostly; like a phantom or an illusion.
The highest point; a tall, pointed mountain peak or the slender spire on a building.
A flat case for carrying loose papers and documents.
An intuitive feeling that something is about to happen.
A territory ruled by a prince.
A clear piece of glass with flat sides that splits light into the colors of the rainbow.
A high point of land jutting out into the sea.
Rose-colored. Also hopeful or overly optimistic.

A small river in northern Italy. Julius Caesar crossed it with his army in 49 B.C., starting a civil war, so “crossing the Rubicon” means passing a point of no return. See Crossing the Rubicon (Ch 23).
A fragrant wood from India and the Pacific, burned as incense and used in perfume.
Having to do with clothing, tailoring, or style of dress.
A person who sees the future; a prophet.
The title of the king of Persia, now Iran.
A swindle in which a pea is hidden under one of three shells or cups and shuffled, and bettors guess where it is. The operator usually palms the pea, so no one can win.
A small, light boat for rowing or sailing. Young’s “skiff moon” is a crescent shaped like one.
A pole used as a ship’s mast, boom, or yard. Spar is also the name for certain shiny, easily split crystalline minerals, such as Iceland spar.
A horse race over fences, ditches, and water jumps, first run cross-country from one church steeple to another.

A woman who campaigned for women’s right to vote. The word was coined by a London newspaper in 1906 for militant British activists. Most American activists called themselves suffragists. See Women’s Suffrage.
A country ruled by a sultan.
Extra; more than the number needed. In the theater, an extra with no lines.
A light four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with two seats, often with a fringed canopy on top.
A formal statement given as evidence or proof of something.
The size or carrying capacity of a ship.
A sluggish, heavy, half-asleep state.
Slang for asking someone for money, especially a small loan. To “make a touch” is to borrow or beg cash.
words.note: The slang sense cannot be searched for; chapters are set by hand.

words.definition: To carry out or carry through. Young uses it for crossing a distance, as in “transacted the gulf between two worlds.”
A change from one form or substance into another, especially the alchemists’ dream of turning base metal into gold.
A small tower on a building or castle.
Impossible to defend, hold, or live in.
A period of staying awake to keep watch, especially at the bedside of someone sick or dying.
